n: Chapters 30–33 are often called the “Book of Consolation”—a cluster of hope-filled prophecies amid Jeremiah’s darker messages.
God tells Jeremiah to write these words down in a book, so the promise will be preserved for people who need it later.
The theme: the day is coming when God will bring both Israel (the northern tribes) and Judah home from captivity to possess their land again.

f.w: I will bring again the captivity
f.g: Or “restore the fortunes”—a key phrase repeated through these chapters.

n: These are the Lord’s words about Israel and Judah.
The scene opens with cries of terror and panic—no peace anywhere.
Strong men are clutching their sides and turning pale, as if they were women in labor. A vivid picture of helpless anguish.
That day will be unlike any other—“the time of Jacob’s trouble.” Yet he will be saved out of it. Latter-day Saints often apply this phrase also to troubles preceding the Second Coming.

f.w: he shall be saved out of it

n: In that day God will break the oppressor’s yoke off Israel’s neck and snap its chains; foreigners will no longer enslave them.

f.w: I will break his yoke from off thy neck

n: Instead, they will serve the Lord their God and “David their king”—not the long-dead David but a future king from his line. Christians see this as the Messiah, Jesus Christ, the Son of David.
Don’t be afraid, Jacob my servant. God will rescue you and your children from distant lands; you will return and live in quiet peace with no one to terrify you.

f.w: fear thou not, O my servant Jacob

n: God will completely destroy the nations where Israel was scattered, but never completely destroy Israel. He will discipline them fairly—not leave them unpunished, but not crush them.

f.w: I will correct thee in measure
will I not make a full end of thee

n: God describes Israel’s condition honestly: the wound is incurable and severe. Human remedies can’t fix the damage sin has done.
No one will defend you or bind up your wound; there is no medicine that can heal you.
All your “lovers”—the foreign allies Judah relied on—have abandoned you. God wounded you like an enemy because your sins were so many.
Why cry about your pain? You brought it on yourself through your many sins. Accepting responsibility is the first step toward healing.
But now the reversal: all who devoured Israel will be devoured; all oppressors will go into captivity; plunderers will be plundered.

f.w: they that spoil thee shall be a spoil

n: The “incurable” wound will be healed by God himself. Because the nations called Zion an outcast that nobody cares about, God will care for her. What no human can heal, God can.

f.w: I will restore health unto thee

n: God will restore Jacob’s homes; the city will be rebuilt on its own ruin-mound, and the palace will stand where it should.

f.g: Hebrew tel—the mound formed by layers of earlier ruins, on which ancient cities were rebuilt.

n: Songs of thanksgiving and celebration will be heard again. God will make them many and honored instead of few and despised.

f.w: the voice of them that make merry

n: Their children will flourish as in former days; their community will be firmly established before God, and oppressors will be punished.

Their ruler will be one of their own, not a foreigner. God will bring him near, and he will approach God—something only a person God invites dares to do. This hints at a priest-king, fulfilled for Christians in Christ.
The covenant is renewed: you will be my people, and I will be your God.

f.w: ye shall be my people, and I will be your God

n: A reminder: the Lord’s storm of judgment is already moving and will crash on the heads of the wicked.
God’s anger will not turn back until his purposes are complete. “In the latter days” you will understand it—the full meaning will be clear in time.

f.w: in the latter days ye shall consider it
